READ 2301.12004v1 | Understanding the Effectiveness of Very Large Language Models on Dialog Evaluation
cat=cs.CL url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12004v1
s[0] Understanding the Effectiveness of Very Large Language Models on Dialog Evaluation Very Large Language Models for Dialog Evaluation J.
s[1] Huynh et al.
s[2] Jessica Huynh Carnegie Mellon University, jhuynh@cs.cmu.edu Cathy Jiao Carnegie Mellon University, cljiao@cs.cmu.edu Prakhar Gupta Carnegie Mellon University, prakharg@cs.cmu.edu Shikib Mehri Amazon, asmehri@amazon.com (work done while at Carnegie Mellon University) Payal Bajaj Microsoft Turing, pabajaj@microsoft.com Vishrav Chaudhary Microsoft Turing,
s[3] vchaudhary@microsoft.com Maxine Eskenazi Carnegie Mellon University, max@cs.cmu.edu * Jessica Huynh, Cathy Jiao, Prakhar Gupta, Shikib Mehri, Payal Bajaj, Vishrav Chaudhary, Maxine Eskenazi January 14, 2024 =========================================================================================================== Language models have steadily increased in size over the past few years.
s[4] They achieve a high level of performance on various natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as question answering and summarization.
s[5] Large language models (LLMs) have been used for generation and can now output human-like text.
s[6] Due to this, there are other downstream tasks in the realm of dialog that can now harness the LLMs' language understanding capabilities.
s[7] Dialog evaluation is one task that this paper will explore.
s[8] It concentrates on prompting with LLMs: BLOOM, OPT, GPT-3, Flan-T5, InstructDial and TNLGv2.
s[9] The paper shows that the choice of datasets used for training a model contributes to how well it performs on a task as well as on how the prompt should be structured.
s[10] Specifically, the more diverse and relevant the group of datasets that a model is trained on, the better dialog evaluation performs.
s[11] This paper also investigates how the number of examples in the prompt and the type of example selection used affect the model's performance.
s[12] § INTRODUCTION In recent years, language models such as GPT-3 <cit.> have grown larger, and their performance on downstream natural language processing (NLP) tasks has significantly improved in low-resource settings where only a few instances per task are available (few-shot).
s[13] The larger these models are, the higher their performances trend on tasks such as language generation and evaluation <cit.>.
s[14] They can generate coherent, fluent and interesting responses.
s[15] However, they can also produce responses that are repetitive and un-engaging <cit.>, in addition to being hard to control.

READ 2301.11916v3 | Large Language Models Are Latent Variable Models: Explaining and Finding Good Demonstrations for In-Context Learning
cat=cs.CL url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11916v3
s[0] [ [ January 14, 2024 ==================== In recent years, pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable efficiency in achieving an inference-time few-shot learning capability known as in-context learning.
s[1] However, existing literature has highlighted the sensitivity of this capability to the selection of few-shot demonstrations.
s[2] Current understandings of the underlying mechanisms by which this capability arises from regular language model pretraining objectives remain disconnected from the real-world LLMs.
s[3] This study aims to examine the in-context learning phenomenon through a Bayesian lens, viewing real-world LLMs as latent variable models.
s[4] On this premise, we propose an algorithm to select optimal demonstrations from a set of annotated data with a small LM, and then directly generalize the selected demonstrations to larger LMs.
s[5] We demonstrate significant improvement over baselines, averaged over eight GPT models on eight real-world text classification datasets.
s[6] We also demonstrate the real-world usefulness of our algorithm on GSM8K, a math word problem dataset.
s[7] Our empirical findings support our hypothesis that LLMs implicitly infer a latent variable containing task information.
s[8] [Code: <https://github.com/WANGXinyiLinda/concept-based-demonstration-selection>.] § INTRODUCTION Transformer-based <cit.> pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant advancements in a variety of natural language processing (NLP) tasks.
s[9] As the size of these LLMs increases, they gain “in-context learning” capabilities, whereby the models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) or near-SOTA performance by conditioning on a small number of demonstration examples at inference time, without any need for updating model parameters <cit.>.
s[10] Below is an example input sequence for semantic analysis with in-context learning: The first two lines are two demonstrations, and the third line is a test input.
s[11] We expect an LLM to output the correct label as a continuation.
s[12] In-context learning has been demonstrated to be an effective technique for a wide range of NLP tasks.
s[13] However, it is sensitive to the choice, format, and even the order of the demonstrations used <cit.>.
s[14] This makes achieving optimal performance with in-context learning a significant challenge, requiring real human effort to adjust the format and selection of demonstration examples.
s[15] Heuristic solutions, such as selecting demonstrations based on the similarity between the demonstrations and test input <cit.> have been proposed, but a comprehensive understanding of why certain demonstrations are effective while others are not remains elusive.
